query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: When synthesizing noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles via rapid heating and cooling, there exists an optimal dwell time and temperature window—positioned above the highest intrinsic nucleation temperature among the constituent metals—that maximizes atomic diffusion enough to drive a controlled disorder-to-order transition while avoiding selective nucleation of early-condensing species. This window balances the intrinsic nucleation temperature differences (dictated by saturation pressures) against kinetic barriers, thus governing the formation of a uniform single-phase solid solution.
generation.material_initial_state: Disordered, solid-solution HEA nanoparticle precursors prepared from mixed metal salt formulations (e.g., PtPdAuFeCoNiCuSn) on a carbon substrate.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, intermediate dwell period at a target temperature (near 1100 K or slightly above the highest nucleation temperature among the metals) after the initial rapid heating pulse. Systematically vary the duration of this dwell period to tune atomic mobility.
generation.conditions: Synthesis performed under rapid thermal cycling conditions (initial heating for tens of milliseconds followed by a secondary dwell period of varied durations and subsequent rapid cooling) for noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements. The experiment should be conducted on a substrate (e.g., carbon) to control heat transfer and particle support, within temperatures where phase separation competes with disorder-to-order transitions.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of atomic ordering and the uniformity of elemental distribution serve as the mediator. Specifically, the establishment of a continuously ordered intermetallic (e.g., L10 type) structure compared to a segregated or phase-separated morphology mediates the observed outcome.
generation.mechanism: During the controlled dwell at the elevated temperature, atoms gain sufficient kinetic energy to overcome local energy barriers, allowing a disorder-to-order transition. However, excessive dwell time permits differential nucleation due to differing saturation pressures, leading to elemental segregation. Thus, a well‐chosen dwell period promotes uniform diffusion and ordering before such differential nucleation begins, effectively 'locking in' the uniform single-phase solid solution upon rapid cooling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline rapid heating/cooling regimen, samples treated with an optimally tuned dwell period will exhibit enhanced single-phase intermetallic ordering, minimal elemental segregation, and controlled particle morphology. Deviations from the optimal dwell time (either too short or too long) will result in either insufficient ordering or increased phase separation.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized using a standard rapid heating (tens of milliseconds), no/short dwell, and ultrarapid cooling protocol which leads to disordered solid solutions with signs of elemental segregation or phase separation in some cases.
generation.boundary: This concept applies primarily to noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles with more than five elements synthesized under rapid thermal shock regimes. It is valid where intrinsic nucleation temperature differences among constituents are pronounced and where synthesis is performed on substrates that moderately influence heat transfer, such as carbon supports.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on the controlled disorder-to-order transition evidence from PMC8797181::web::003 and PMC8797181::web::005 (demonstrating a 5-minute dwell at ~1100 K yields ordered MPEI nanoparticles) combined with the plasma synthesis observations from PMC10873330::web::003 (showing that differences in elemental saturation pressures lead to segregation). What is new is the explicit proposal to systematically map the dwell time versus ordering/segregation balance in noble metal HEA systems, including quantifying the threshold at which atomic mobility shifts from beneficial to detrimental.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of nanoparticle syntheses that are identical in composition and overall thermal history except for the duration of the intermediate dwell period (e.g., 0 ms (baseline), 2 min, 5 min, 8 min). Characterize the resulting nanoparticles using XRD, HAADF-STEM and elemental mapping (e.g., EDS) to assess phase ordering and elemental distribution. Compare the degree of atomic ordering and segregation as a function of dwell time.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to determine phase uniformity and crystallographic ordering
High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) for nanoparticle morphology
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping for assessing elemental segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant improvement in single-phase ordering (i.e., reduced segregation and uniform intermetallic ordering) is observed at any intermediate dwell time compared to the baseline synthesis, or if longer dwell times do not lead to a systematic progression from disordered to ordered states before phase separation appears, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. To address the above challenge, we propose an ultrafast (<100 ms), one-step method for the continuous synthesis of HEA NPs directly from a mixture of pure elemental metal powders by using a thermal plasma jet. Thermal plasma jets are partially ionized gases with high temperature (>8000 K) and high speed. They are capable of rapid heating of feedstock to produce an atomically mixed multi-component vapor, and also rapid cooling of the vapor at an ultrahigh cooling rate of 105 − 106 K s−1 to form solid-solution particles. Feedstock can be injected continuously, thus this technology is well suited for scalable synthesis of HEA NPs. Despite this unique potential, thermal plasma jets have only been used for the processing of bulk HEAs or spheroidization of pre-alloyed HEA powders. The main challenge would be the existence of a large nucleation temperature gap among different metal vapors; upon plasma jet cooling, the element with the lowest saturation vapor pressure reaches the supersaturated state first and segregates.

In this work, we demonstrate the synthesis of nanoscale MPEIs (4 to 5 nm) that contain up to eight different elements without particle growth or phase separation via a unique multi-elemental disorder-to-order (HEA to MPEI) phase transition strategy (Fig. 1A). Specifically, we first rapidly Joule-heated metal salt precursors on the carbon substrate [x-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy characterization in fig. S2] at ~1100 K for 55 ms to produce disordered solid-solution HEA nanoparticles as the starting material (). We then use the precise heating control made possible by this Joule-heating approach (in which the reaction temperature is controlled by an electric current) to reheat the HEA nanoparticles for just 5 min at ~1100 K to promote atomic rearrangement to a more thermodynamically stable MPEI configuration (i.e., a disorder-to-order transition), followed by rapid cooling to lock the final ordered structure in place. The resulting MPEI nanoparticles feature an intermetallic structure that has two sublattices (A1B1) (fig. S3a). To synthesize the MPEI nanoparticles, we preloaded a carbon substrate with desired metal salt precursor combinations/ratios and Joule-heated (fig. S5) the materials with precise control of the temperature and heating/cooling rates by tuning the power applied to the substrate (fig. S6). The temperature profile and structural evolution of nanoparticles over time are illustrated in Fig. 2A. We first synthesize solid-solution (HEA) nanoparticles () by heating the metal precursors for tens of milliseconds at ~1100 K. This is a critical step for mixing the different elements without phase separation. A disorder-to-order phase transition is then achieved by rapidly reheating the materials to ~1100 K for an additional ~5 min—a limited amount of time that is sufficient to complete the desired transition from the disordered HEA structure to the ordered, single-phase MPEI configuration while simultaneously avoiding nanoparticle growth/agglomeration. Last, the single-phase MPEI structure and small particle size (~5 nm) is preserved by rapidly cooling the materials (~104 K/s).

We also simulated this disorder-to-order phase transition through MC modeling () of the atomic arrangement of the quinary Pt(Fe0.7Co0.1Ni0.1Cu0.1) nanoparticle at 1100 K (Fig. 4A and movie S1), which shows the atoms of the disordered HEA starting material diffusing to form the ordered MPEI, similar to the transition process in other intermetallics (, ). During the transition, the formation enthalpy (ΔHf) of the quinary MPEI decreases substantially (Fig. 4B), driven by the strong interaction via the spin-orbit coupling and the hybridization between non-noble metal 3d and noble 5d states. The decreased enthalpy leads to a lower Gibbs free energy of the MPEI (Go) than that of the HEA (Gd) sample (based on the same quinary composition PtFe0.7Co0.1Ni0.1Cu0.1) at a wide temperature range (~273 to 1500 K), according to MC modeling (Fig. 4C). At temperatures below 1500 K (and above the decomposition temperature of the metal salts; table S8), the low enthalpy of the MPEIs dominates the Gibbs free energy and thus Go < Gd.
